utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ceklic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ceklic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I must congratulate you. You are the first and the second in a series of 100 witnesses. You're number 101. I must ask you and remind myself, too, that we should speak slowly and pause between question and answer so that everything can be recorded. Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D7899.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see the statement in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please show us the last page with the signature. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team, or does anything need to be changed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the statement was faithfully rendered and there is no need to change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you the same questions today, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The essence would not change at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under Rule 92 ter, I seek to tender the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're offering three associated exhibits listed in our 92 ter notice, and we would ask that for each of them they be added to our Rule 65 ter list as we didn't have them at the time that list was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No, no objections, just an observation. Document 1D14009, referenced at paragraph 37, has been admitted. It's D1193. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we'll receive the statement as well as the remaining two associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The 92 ter statement 1D7899 will be D3112, and the other two associated exhibits will be D3113 and D3114 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read the summary of Mr. Momcilo Ceklic's statement in English. [In English] Momcilo Ceklic was born on the 23rd of September, 1941, in Obrinje village, Kalinovik municipality. He is a lawyer by profession and currently resides in east Novo Sarajevo. He was the secretary of the Ilidza Municipal Assembly and a member of the Crisis Staff. Following the establishment of the HDZ and SDA municipal parties in 1990, the SDS Municipal Board was formed on 7th of September, 1990. After the multi-party elections in November 1990, Mr. Momcilo Ceklic observed relations between the parties deteriorated as interethnic tensions continued to mount in the area. In one instance in May 1991, the taxi drivers of Sarajevo drove throughout Serbian areas of Ilidza with Muslim markings, making noise and firing shots. It was a public secret that the Muslims were preparing for war. Momcilo Ceklic himself witnessed between 150 to 200 Muslims undergoing training at this time. The Ilidza settlement of Sokolovic Kolonija was a stronghold of the SDA and its paramilitary formations. On January the 2nd, 1992, the Ilidza SDS Municipal Board formed a Crisis Staff, and on the following day, the SDS proclaimed the Serbian Ilidza municipality, which was intended for preventive and political activities. The Crisis Staff did not hold a sessions -- session until early April, despite the difficulty security situation. In the following period, persecution and arrests of Serbs began in Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija, predominantly Muslim settlements of Ilidza municipality. Serbian deputies in the BH Assembly were out-voted, and Muslims and Croatian deputies proclaimed the independence of BH against the will of the Serbian people. In early March 1992, Muslim forces carried out an armed attack on a nearby Serbian settlement and seized the Novi Grad and Novo Sarajevo police stations. Alija Izetbegovic declared a general mobilisation, engaging and arming Muslim forces, including the Green Berets paramilitary units. In light of these events, the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality Ilidza adopted a decision to place a defence around the Serbian settlements in order in order to protect the Serbian people. On 5th of April, 1992, the constitutive session of the Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza took place. The Assembly proclaimed a state of imminent threat of war and authorised the commander of the Crisis Staff to adopt decisions, orders, and instructions on behalf of the Assembly. Following a Muslim attack on Ilidza on April the 22nd, the Crisis Staff adopted a decision on to declare a state of war in Ilidza municipality. Throughout this period, the Crisis Staff made a number of attempts to negotiate for lasting peace but received no co-operation from the Muslim side, and the conflict continued to escalate throughout 1992. In one incident, Momcilo Ceklic witnessed Muslim forces fire missiles on a bus station in Ilidza, killing and wounding several civilians. The Crisis Staff was formed pursuant to the instructions of the government of the Serbian Republic of BH with the intention of taking over the prerogatives and functions of the Municipal Assembly when it was unable to meet. Representatives of the government of the Serbian Republic of BH appointed by the government played a co-ordinative role for them to act professionally and in accordance with the law. It was not a means to remove members of the other nationalities from the territory of BH in any inhumane method. During the fighting that followed, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs fled Ilidza, and some returned for the duration of the war, including Muslims and Croats. All civilians, regardless of their ethnicity, were allowed freedom of movement. Momcilo Ceklic had no knowledge of any camps for prisoners of war or collection centre in his territory, except for one semiopen pre-war prison used to house Croatian and Muslim prisoners of war as well as Serbian prisoners. It was never the policy of the SDS generally to permanently remove Muslims and Croats from BH in Serbian regions, and genocide, persecution, extermination, deportation, and other inhumane acts were not propagated by the SDS staff. Dr. Radovan Karadzic could not have taken any unilateral decisions in the SDS, nor did he display such tendencies. The municipalities were independent, and their relationship with the president of the Republika Srpska was in accordance with a valid constitutional and legal provisions. With regards to Ilidza, it was cut off from the influence of higher organs of power throughout the war because it was under enemy encirclement. There was no control, and the course of events was decided by situation. Momcilo Ceklic was aware of the existence of paramilitaries that formed in the chaotic beginnings of the war, but they were not tolerated by the Serbian municipality of Ilidza authorities which did its best to remove them and impose order. [Interpretation] This was a brief summary of Mr. Momcilo Ceklic's statement summary. I have no further questions to the witness at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ceklic, as you have noted from Mr. Karadzic's comments that your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ceklic. At paragraph 12 of your statement you said that the HDZ formed a municipality in the Stup settlement of Ilidza and that on the 3rd of January, the SDS analogously proclaimed the Serbian Ilidza municipality. Now, that suggests that this step taken by the Ilidza SDS was an independent local initiative, and in fact the decision to form a Serbian municipality in Ilidza was based at least in part on SDS Main Board instructions of 19 December 1991, otherwise known as the Variant A and B instructions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: I must tell you that the Croats in their area, that is at Stup 1 and Stup 2, were the first ones in Bosnia-Herzegovina who established their own municipality, and as a response the Serbs proclaimed the Assembly of the Serbian people on the 3rd of January, 1992. This Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza, which was proclaimed on the 3rd of January, 1992, was purely fictitious, which means that it didn't do anything special. It had a preventive political character.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but my question was simply whether or not you agree that the Serbian municipality of Ilidza was formed, at least in part, based on SDS Main Board instructions of the -- of 19 December 1991. Do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was partly established based on that instruction, but that instruction was never fully implemented, never fully honoured.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And at paragraph 37 of your statement you talked about the creation of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza, and you state that the Crisis Staff was formed on the basis of the government instructions, and you refer to P2717, and those instructions are dated the 26th of April, 1992. And the document reflecting the creation of the Crisis Staff also referenced in your -- in that paragraph of your statement is D1193, and that document is dated the 10th of April, 1992. Now, you agree with me, don't you, that it's impossible for the -- it would have been impossible for the Serbian municipality of Ilidza to form a Crisis Staff on the 10th of April, 1992, on the basis of instructions that were only issued 16 days later, on the 26th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Speaking about Crisis Staffs in the Ilidza municipality, we must distinguish between two types: One was the party's Crisis Staff, which was established on 2nd of January, 1992, and it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ceklic, I'm aware of that distinction. I'm just referring to assertions that you have made in your statement, and your assertion at paragraph 37 is that the Serbian municipality created a Crisis Staff, and the document you've referenced for that is dated the 10th of April, 1992. You've also asserted that that Crisis Staff was formed based on the government instructions that were dated 16 days later, the 26th of April, 1992. Now, you agree with me that that's impossible?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: I think I understood you well. The Crisis Staff was formed pursuant to the instruction dated 19 December 1991. Maybe this is a play on words in the statement. The Crisis Staff was established following the instructions of 19 December 1991. Now the dates fit, and that date is actually the right one. Do you understand? Because there was a Crisis Staff that was a party's Crisis Staff of 3 January 1992, and another Crisis Staff with a different structure was established on 10 April, 1992, and this Crisis Staff in the true sense of the word is some type of a local government body which had -- which executed the duties of the municipality, although the municipality could not do its proper work. The situation at Ilidza throughout the war was very specific, because the Municipal Assembly and the municipal structures functioned almost throughout the war, and the Crisis Staff was one kind of co-ordination between the municipal bodies and the government bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you again, but I think we're moving away from my question. Now, I understand your position now to be that both Crisis Staffs were based -- were formed on the basis of the 19 December 1991 instructions. Were you aware that at the 14th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 27th of March, 1992, Karadzic instructed the deputies to establish Crisis Staffs in their municipalities, and that's D304, page 20?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: I was never aware of such instructions, and I doubt that Mr. Karadzic would have issued such an instruction of his own accord. He is a great democrat, and all the main decisions were taken by the Main Board at the level of the Serbian Republic. Mr. Karadzic can make proposals, but the decisions were taken by the Main Board which was a collective organ of authority. It decided in a democratic fashion. In the Main Board it was not Mr. Karadzic who could take decisions on his own. I'm not aware of any such instruction issued by Mr. Karadzic. Finally, he never showed an inclination to do anything of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I won't take that any further except to just confirm that you never attended the Bosnian Serb Assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: I never attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: I attended some of their meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, you said you never attend, and then you said I attended some of their meetings. Did you ever attend any meetings of the Bosnian Serb Assembly at the republic level?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: No, no. There must be a misunderstanding. I never attended the Assembly sessions at the republic level, but I did attend meetings of the Crisis Staff at the municipal level because it was part of my duties. I was referring to the local level.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ceklic. I'm going to ask you to please keep your answers as short and directed to the question as possible because I have very limited time. Okay. In your statement you talk about how the Muslims were preparing for war, including by arming, and I refer, for example, to paragraph 13, but it's true, is it not, that the Serb authorities in Ilidza undertook intense activity to arm citizens of Serbian nationality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're interested in first and foremost about the arming of the Muslims or the arming of the Serbs. The Serbs never prepared for war. They only prepared for defence, because the policy of the Serb leadership and the SDS at the level of the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina was directed at --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ceklic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: -- the preservation of the biological and physical survival of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you again, but I wasn't asking you about policies. I was just asking you whether you agreed or disagreed with the proposition that prior to the war the Serb authorities in Ilidza undertook intense activity to arm citizens of Serbian nationality. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: The arming of the Serbs only started once the Muslims had started to arm themselves, and this arming process was based on weapons from the Territorial Defence, to a very minor degree to -- on weapons from the JNA's warehouses. From Donji Potok somewhere in early April when the MUP -- MUP's warehouse was placed under control, then weapons were distributed to the Serbian people. But it was clear that all the goings-on would result in war. There couldn't have been any other outcome.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Krtelj was not recorded. Perhaps the witness could explain what that is. But it was not recorded that the Muslims took Krtelj.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement you refer in a number of places to attacks by Muslim forces in Ilidza. You refer to an all-out attack on Ilidza on the 22nd of April. That's paragraph 25. An attack on Rakovica settlement on the 27th of April, paragraph 32. Another all-out attack on Ilidza on the 14th of May, paragraph 33. And at paragraph 35 you make the general assertion that Ilidza was subjected to constant Muslim attacks, that the Serbian forces were constantly defending their lines, and they did not have any aspirations to conquer territory under Muslim control. Now, first with respect to the two all-out attacks you refer to on the 22nd of April and the 14th of May, Bosnian Serb forces not only repelled those attacks but conquered new territory in the course of them, and Bosnian Serb forces in Ilidza carried out a number of offensive operations resulting in conquering territory held by Muslims; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: No. Absolutely false. It is only correct that the first attack on the Serbian population of Ilidza happened on the 25th of April at a quarter before 6.00. Ilidza was attacked from all directions, Sokolovic Kolonija, Butmir, Hrasnica, Stupsko Brdo, and so on, and there was heavy fighting that went on for about 12 hours. Once they repelled the Muslim attack, the Serbs stayed in their area without any ambitions to conquer other territories. The Serbs never had such ambitions. That is completely false. Eleven people were killed, 56 were wounded. Then -- but unfortunately -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you again. Your position is clear that my proposition I put to you is completely false, and I'm not interested at the moment in the details of these operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P2308, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a report from the 20th of September, 1993, from the Ilidza public security station to the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 in both the languages.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Could you please turn up the volume. The volume, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The usher will be coming to assist you, Mr. Ceklic. Do you hear me well now, Mr. Ceklic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If you could look towards the bottom half of this page. It refers to the two attacks that you describe three paragraphs from the bottom, the attack on the 22nd of April, 1992, and then in the next paragraph another attack on the 14th of May, 1992, and then at the bottom of the page it says that: "Organisation of the defence in the above-mentioned cases was done by Mr. Kovac and his associates. It was very successful, which is confirmed by the fact that the enemy didn't gain any of our territory while we conquered new territory ..." And then if we go to the next page, it says: "Offensive actions undertaken by the members of the public security station resulting in new territories under our control are as follows..." And then there is a rather extensive list on page 5. 13th of May, it says Binjezevo was liberated joining Hadzici to Ilidza. From the 15th of May to the 31st of May, Rakovica local municipality was liberated, again joining territories. 1st of March, liberation of Ahatovici, referred to as a Muslim strategic point. The 9th of June, 1992, there's a mistake in the English translation, refers to a successful action in Kasindolska Street. 17th of June, liberation of airport settlement, liberation of Doglodi, member -- the conquering of the shopping centre Cenex. It's clear from this document, isn't it, Mr. Ceklic, that there were a number of offensive operations aimed at conquering new territories by Bosnian Serb forces in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we talked about the first attack on the 22nd of April, and I told you about what transpired on the 22nd of April. Everything else that you went on to read was beyond the 22nd of April, at a later date. The 22nd of April was before, and I was talking about that, when a Muslim attack was staved off, the attack on Ilidza. The Serbs kept the status quo and held onto their own territory. Everything you have enumerated happened after the 22nd of April. So -- I've never heard all of this information before. Talking about Rakovica, because that's what you mentioned, it never needed to be liberated because it was part of the Ilidza municipality. It could only have been viewed as active defence and certainly not as an ambition to conquer territory that was predominantly Muslim. I'm not sure if we have understanding here. I am certainly doing my best to be perfectly clear on these issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. So I'm telling you what I know about the 22nd of April as someone who was there and who was a first-hand witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ceklic. I'd like to stay on this document for a moment and move to another topic which is the statement that you made at paragraph 27 that people fled Ilidza in panic and fear during the fighting and that there was no organised or forced expulsions or ethnic cleansing. Now, first it's true that the Serb police in Ilidza were detaining Muslims and taking repressive measures against them resulting -- causing them to flee, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: No, it's not true. That's simply not what happened. I need to explain one thing. When there is a war on, what you have is chaos all over the place. Everybody fears for their own personal safety and that of their families. It wasn't just the Muslims that were fleeing Ilidza at the time but Serbs and Croats, too, leaving four predominantly Croat, Serb, and Muslim areas. Serbs, too, were leaving for Montenegro and Serbia. My own family was in Serbia at the time, and that applied to quite a number of people there. So it wasn't just that the Muslims were leaving. You have people from all three ethnic groups leaving the area because of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ceklic. It's --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: May I just add one thing if I may?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. Your answer to my question was very clear. I have limited time. I just don't have time for you to give me all these details. It's clear that you deny that the police were taking repressive measures against detained Muslims causing them to flee.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 of this document, please, and this is again the report from the Ilidza public security station to the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the second paragraph from the bottom states that: "All detained Muslims were thoroughly interrogated in order to extract useful information regarding their intentions. Repressive measures undertaken against them for various reasons resulted in them increasingly fleeing and moving out of this territory." So it's right here in black and white from the Serbian police station in Ilidza itself; isn't that right, Mr. Ceklic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: There is one thing that you need to know: I wasn't up to date on the Ilidza police station reports. I have a rough understanding of how the situation evolved in terms of any population movements and people leaving Ilidza for other areas. As for police-generated information, you must understand that I wasn't privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. Now, staying on the same topic but moving to another part of your statement, you referred at paragraph 30 to an incident at that took place during negotiations that were taking place on the 23rd of April, 1992, and you said that Muslims opened fire on Serbian areas from Gornji and Donji Kotorac. And then you said that the JNA returned fire and in the ensuing search of these settlements weapons were seized, the biggest extremists were taken to Kula, while civilians from these settlements fled to Butmir and Dobrinja. Now, it's true, is it not, that after this 23rd of April operation the Muslim civilians who had fled Gornji Kotorac returned? Then on the 12th of May, 1992, on the order of Mr. Prstojevic, the women and children were expelled to Sarajevo and the men were imprisoned in Kula. And a few days later, those men, too, were expelled. And this is another example of the organised expulsion of non-Serbs from Ilidza. Do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: I disagree. This is entirely erroneous. Gornji Kotorac had a total of 70 Muslim households more or less. This was prior to the 23rd of April, 1992. There were frequent acts of provocation from Gornji Kotorac against Kasindol and the Lukavica barracks. So they had no choice but to respond and deduce some form of control throughout that area where quite a large quantity of weapons was found. There was fire being opened at the barracks in Lukavica and Kasindol, and that was causing a lot of problems. So these people were taken to the Kula KP Dom and kept there for a while. There were no women and children there being kept at this correctional facility. The only people being held there were Muslim extremists who were frequently opening fire on those positions. Secondly, you couldn't say that these civilians were expelled. They left on their own accord. The simple reason being they were afraid because weapons were found in the position of their fellow Muslims in their homes. They were now taken to the Kula KP Dom. So the women and children now became scared, and they left Kotorac because of that. It's not that they were driven out. Nobody was forced to stay. Everybody was -- who was forced to leave. Everybody was allowed to stay. Some left, but some returned even during the war, and some even spent the whole duration of the war in Ilidza. Therefore, Madam Prosecutor, I think what you just specified is entirely erroneous, and I can say that without any kind of bias at all. Even the military-aged men who returned eventually began to pursue their activities in terms of opening fire, using all kinds of different weapons to cause unrest. I believe it was on or about the 12th of May that something like that reoccurred just prior to the 14th of April attack on Ilidza, the second attack. So they continued to pester the military and the Serbian settlements there. There was no other way but to do something about it. People involved in such extreme activities had to be removed in order for the situation to go back to normal to some extent at least. That is the only truth, and everything else is just speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Your position is clear. If we could go to P1086, please. This is a transcript of a conversation between Mr. Prstojevic and a certain Milenko, then a certain Novakovic, and although it's dated the 14th of May, 1992, there's evidence from Mr. Prstojevic that it should be -- that this conversation actually took place on the 12th of May, and that's at transcript page 13859. And towards the bottom of the page, Mr. -- or at the top of the next page in the B/C/S, I apologise, the bottom of page 1 in the English, Mr. Prstojevic says: "Why did Mika phone me?" And Milenko says: "To check with you these people in Kotorac. What should we do with them?" And Mr. Prstojevic says: "Did you arrest them? What did you do?" And if we turn the page in the English, Milenko says: "People are down there." And Prstojevic asks again: "Have they been arrested?" And then Milenko says a couple of lines down: "Down there on the road all of them, men are separated from women." And then Milenko again a few lines down says: "I just received the word men are in the Kula prison and women went in the direction of Butmir." And then Novakovic comes on the phone, and if we go to the next page in the B/C/S, Prstojevic asks Novakovic: "Have you been cleaning Kotorac today?" And Novakovic says: "They have. I don't note exact details." And then a few lines down Prstojevic says: "That's okay, but tell me, please, I beg of you, why did you take women to Butmir?" And Novakovic says: "They said women were not in Butmir." And then he clarifies: "Well, in Butmir, yes, not to KP Dom but to Butmir. That's where they're going." And Prstojevic says: "They cannot go to Butmir. We'll mop up Butmir in time as well." And then the next page in English, Prstojevic says: "Butmir will be mopped up, Sokolovic will be mopped up, Hrasnica will be mopped up." And Novakovic says: "Well, I don't know where to take them." And Prstojevic says: "They will all -- there is Bascarsija? Please take all of them to Bascarsija on foot," and he clarifies, "women, and men to prison." And then Novakovic says: "Okay. I'll check with them and I'll let you know." And Prstojevic says: "Tell them those who convert to Orthodox religion on the spot, they can stay, women and children." And then they sign off.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could now go to P1126.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask one thing. Could we have fewer of these really complex questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I haven't asked my question yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At P1126 is a memo from the Ilidza -- sorry, the Kula police station to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Ministry of Justice dated the 20th of May, and it says that since the 12th of May until the 20th of May there are 156 persons detained in KPD Butmir, and in the next paragraph it says that 38 persons were brought in by the Ilidza TO who were in possession of automatic weapons in Kasindolska Street, and then it says: "47 persons from Gornji Kotorac removed in an operation by former JNA and TO Kasindol forces but returned to the area of Gornji Kotorac on the 12th of May and were therefore taken to KPD Butmir." And then it goes on to refer to other people taken from Dobrinja and Nedzarici, Vraca, et cetera. And then on the next page of the English it refers to the inadequate conditions in the prison and the need to urgently resolve the status of these detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could finally go to P1151.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I perhaps comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'll ask you a question after I show you one more document, Mr. Ceklic. And this is another letter from the Ilidza Kula police station dated five days after their previous one, and it refers to their previous letter again addressed to the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of the Interior, and it refers to the problems of accommodation from the previous letter, and then in the next paragraph it says: "After co-ordinating with the minister of justice and the SJB undersecretary on the 20th of May, 114 persons were taken to the Vrbanja Bridge location and sent into the city. This group consisted of persons whose place of residence was in Gornji Kotorac and Dobrinja." And then it says that they had unsuccessful communications with the Ilidza exchange bureau, so they decided to send these detainees to the -- to Sarajevo, and then it refers to the need to resolve the status of the 38 persons taken in from Kasindolska Street who were in possession of automatic weapons, hand grenades, and it states had extreme views and therefore should not be exchanged. Now, as these documents show, the Muslim civilians from Gornji Kotorac who returned to Gornji Kotorac on the 12th of May were expelled; the women and children were sent directly to Bascarsija, the men were detained at Kula, and they, too, a few days later were sent into Muslim-held Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, Mr. President, that's like a bar examination question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let's see how the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: How could he possibly remember all the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If he does not remember, then he can say he cannot remember that. Let us see. Yes, Mr. Ceklic, do you remember the question, or should I ask her to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the question is a bit too comprehensive. Perhaps it would be more effective to ask a series of questions subsumed under this one huge large-scale question. But if we have sufficient time, perhaps I could shed some light on this. As for these orders, I'm really not privy to that. As for the KP Dom, again I did not have any direct knowledge of how it operated. All I know is the accounts of some people and witnesses who were there and were released. They stated themselves for the record that they fared much better at the KP Dom than in their own homes and that the care there was better. It's an incontrovertible fact that given the wartime conditions, the conditions at the KP Dom were good, and the professionals there, it is my deepest conviction, worked in keeping with all the rules governing the work and existence of that institution also in terms of prisoner treatment. As for Kotorac and women and children being driven out, I cannot accept that assertion. Not a single person was ever driven out of Ilidza regardless of their ethnicity. People were leaving because they feared for their own personal safety and that of their families. So it was only to be expected that those people would be heading for predominantly Muslim, Serb, or Croat areas as it were. The reference here obviously is to the Muslims. Furthermore, no women or children or indeed pregnant women were ever locked up in the KP Dom at Kula. That is entirely untrue and cannot be maintained as simple as that. I was the Assembly secretary. I -- I worked in an office, but I did know quite a lot of things about a number of different things that were going on at the time, and that's what I can share with you today. People being driven out, no way.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, were you aware at the time that Mr. Prstojevic had a conversation about what to do with people in Gornji Kotorac and he instructed that the women and children be sent to Bascarsija on foot unless they converted to the Orthodox religion on the spot and the men were to be taken to the Kula prison? Did you know about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time. I've heard about it somewhat later. This is anti-rhetoric, though. Mr. Prstojevic said a lot of things and said many more things than he actually ended up doing. I don't think this was done. I think he was just talking a lot. But he's an honourable man, and I think if push ever came to shove, he would have been the first to take a stand and say that no one was to be driven out. This is anti-rhetoric. It's as simple as that. He was just being carried away by the general war atmosphere if you ask me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you deny then that the men were -- were taken to Kula prison in accordance with Mr. Prstojevic's instructions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: I am not denying anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: I am not denying that there were men in prison because of all the reasons that I enumerated but not for the reasons stated by Mr. Prstojevic. Mr. Prstojevic said a lot of things, but none of that ever came to be. He was just shooting his mouth off for the sake of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ceklic, the Chamber has received substantial evidence of Mr. Prstojevic's involvement in military matters in Ilidza and the surroundings, and I would refer, for example, to P5710, P5705, P2411, and P5690. First, were you aware of Mr. Prstojevic's military role at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: No. No. Mr. Prstojevic had links to the civilian authorities and no more than that. There was some co-ordination between these various bodies at Ilidza municipality level, but it was all about the normal operation of all the relevant authorities in Ilidza municipal territory. The people in charge of the military were professionals, Territorial Defence likewise, police likewise, qualified, appropriately skilled people who knew their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd just like to cover one last topic briefly with you which is the topic of paramilitaries. At paragraphs 45 and 46 of your statement, you said that the paramilitaries were not tolerated by the army, the MUP, or the Serbian municipality of Ilidza and that the municipality tried their best to have them removed. If we could go to P5691, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 22 -- or, rather, page 22, line 16, it should read "honourable man."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a transcript a conversation, Mr. Ceklic, on the 13th of May between Captain Legija, one of Arkan's men, and Milisav Gagovic, who at the time was commander of the JNA 4th Corps in Sarajevo, and this is a brief conversation. After the introductions, Gagovic asks: "What's up?" And Legija says: "Well, these men here are kind of trying to get up there towards those through Kasindolska Street to the airport, and those people they were fighting ferociously, but this very centre of Ilidza, these parts of the municipality, I don't know." Gagovic asks: "Okay. Are they falling? Is it possible to monitor where these shells are coming from?" And then a few lines down, Legija says: "I'm going to place my monitors up there."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Gagovic says -- and Gagovic says: "Go ahead and have the monitor report about where the shells are falling. I can cover it all from here from the airport." And then Legija says, and this is at the next page in the B/C/S: "Well, I am going to place my monitors now. And these things coming down from Igman - and there they have those - I know mortars. If I catch their fire, I will send you their grid references up there." And Gagovic says: "Go ahead and do it now." Now, were you aware, Mr. Ceklic, of this kind of co-ordination of military activities between the commander of the JNA 4th Corps and Arkan's men in reference to operations in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: No. First I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to P2229.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a conversation between Mico Stanisic and Nedjeljko Zugic from the 15th of May, 1992. And again it's a very short conversation. And after the introductions, Stanisic says about halfway down the page: "What are you doing?" Zugic says: "I've just come from Sokolac." And a few lines down, Mico Stanisic says: "Good. And where are you now?" And Zugic responds: "I'm in the Serb municipality of Ilidza." "And Stanisic says: "Tell me what the situation is like." Zugic says: "With Vuk and Mlaco and Prstojevic." And on the next page in English, Stanisic says: "Tell me what the situation is like over there." And Zugic says: "Well, we got reinforcements from Gagovic. Some Arkanovci and Seseljevci came. I don't know." And Stanisic says: "Good." Again, were you aware at the time of this kind of approval that the minister of interior gave to the presence of Arkan and Seselj's men in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: I know these men, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zugic, but I wasn't privy to this information. I don't know anything about it. Unless you want to know about the paramilitary units and groups. Perhaps I could should some light on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ceklic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very briefly. Can we please leave the last document -- or, rather, return the last document to our screen. P2229.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please look at the second to last thing here. "Well, we have received reinforcements from Gagovic." Could you tell us, this person Gagovic, he was an officer in which army exactly? Who was around on the 15th of May in your area?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: He was a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know anything about the relationship between the army and -- on one hand and the volunteers and paramilitaries on the other following the 12th of May when Republika Srpska VRS was established?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, Mr. President, the paramilitary units and volunteer units that arrived in Ilidza were people who were not known to us, and they caused more damage to the Serbian people in Ilidza than any good that they may have done. There was no benefit to their presence at all for us. The regular military units and the police tried to drive those units out of Ilidza, but the MUP and the public security station in Ilidza was facing a dire situation because they were running out of equipment and weapons. Could you call those paramilitary units? I don't know. That may be a bit too harsh. These weren't real units. They were just minor groups normally numbering between 10 and 20 men. They would only stick around for a very short while. They would loot the areas around whenever and wherever they could, and they would simply leave, flee Ilidza with whatever it was that they took. Now excuse me, Mr. President. The military and the police were doing their best to place those paramilitary units under control, which was difficult to do, particularly after the date you specified when a certain number of people, a great minority, reported, volunteered with the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the distance between the war zone and Gornji Kotorac, Ilidza, and the settlements that we have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies from right in the middle of Ilidza, across Hrasnica and Vojkovic, I don't know, perhaps 1.000 metres. Nonetheless, for us to reach those areas, the eastern part of Ilidza, we had to take a round about route of about 120, 140 kilometres. So Ilidza was in the thick of the war throughout its duration and the siege was far fiercer than that of Muslim Sarajevo, and this is one thing that people tend to forget these days. Ilidza was under siege for the duration of the war. And it was because of that siege, Mr. President, that we were unable to have a normal communication with the eastern reaches of our municipality. We had take a 140-kilometre round about route in order to get there, whereas as the crow flies the actual distance was no more than a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And what about Gornji Kotorac? Where were the confrontation lines in relation to these villages and how far were those from the theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: The distance between those positions was not particularly great. I think between 150 and 200 metres. No more than that separating the confrontation lines. If I understand you correctly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now tell us, please, as a lawyer you must know this, what are the obligations? Are there certain obligations of the army that is in combat and fighting towards civilians in the areas that are affected by the combat?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly each army in keeping with the international law is supposed to treat civilians in a humane way to comply with the Geneva Conventions and the rules of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about evacuations? Does it have the right or the duty -- or, rather, is it allowed to keep the civilians in the areas where combat is going on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: No. It's not allowed to do that. They can move them perhaps if certain conditions are met.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just one more question. There were some measures mentioned here. Now, as a lawyer, can you tell us whether there are any measures that are envisaged by law? Well, repressive measures envisaged by law.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Well, the repressive measures are there in order to prevent crimes being committed. For instance, in our areas we had a historic session of the Assembly of the Ilidza municipality of the Serbian people on the 28th of August where certain decisions and conclusions were adopted to the effect that all relevant structures may carry out their normal duties, including the army, the police, the prosecutor's office, the judiciary, and so on. So at this session, the special focus was placed on the prevention of crime, because there were frequently instances where state public property was damaged, so there were calls for those perpetrators to be prosecuted and for the prosecution and the judiciary that at that time were functioning well to take measures in keeping with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What are the criteria that the Muslims took? Or actually what was Krtelj --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a base of the Muslims. On the 3rd and 4th of April, Muslim Specials captured Krtelj and then they informed the Muslim forces that there would be convoys arriving from Sarajevo, entire convoys with weapons in order to arm of the Muslim people. That's a generally known fact. This was on the 3rd and 4th of April, 1991, and at the same time in this area sometime in the middle of the night around 12.30 they -- Muslims with some four APCs were prepared to capture Krtelj. So this is to do with the arming and with the movement of these forces. So this was their main base, the main Muslim base which was used for arming the Muslim people. Although there were other people who armed themselves via private channels, also taking weapons away from the TO depots and depots of JNA units. So they've started arming themselves very early on, perhaps early in 1991. Unfortunately, that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to read out to you a brief portion on Mr. Prstojevic's position. This is dated the 4th of May or the 1st of May 1992, D10206. He says as follows: "We also stress that the Serbian authorities of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza provide -- allow free movement of civilians across the territory of this municipality irrespective of their ethnic party, gender, or any other affiliation. All of this, of course, provided that there is police control at check-points." Now, how does this tally with what you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, until the first attack on the 21st of April, 1992, all citizens of Ilidza could move freely, because our check-points, metaphorically speaking, I may say, were rather elastic. So there was absolutely no obstacle to freely moving along those roads. Now, as of the 21st of April, when the first attack on Ilidza was, the only persons who were free to move -- who were allowed to move freely were able bodied men of Serb ethnicity who had to stay there because -- for the purpose of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the basis for arresting able-bodied Muslims? Were all Muslims, able bodied Muslims in Ilidza? Were they all called up and taken to the police station to be questioned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Well, no, not everybody was called to report to the police station. Only extremists, people who had weapons, who harassed the Serbian population and military targets. All other citizens who just behaved like any normal reasonable people, of course, they wouldn't have to be detained or brought to the police station for questioning, nor did we want for something like that to be done. There was no decision of the Municipal Assembly, the War Presidency. What -- adopted in that sense -- in that sense, nor was it ever -- nor was anything like that ever ordered by the top leadership, including yourself, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ceklic, how did they distinguish the extremists from ordinary people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was very simple. An extremist is a person who keeps opening fire on Serb areas against the Serbian population, who opens fire at the Yugoslav People's Army, and the police. I don't know what else you could call it. It's either an extremist or an aggressor. Probably aggressor rather than extremist. And when these people were checked, that's where large quantities of weapons were found, and there were lists of all the weapons that had been seized. And it is for this reason that these people were brought in and kept at the penal and correctional facility at Butmir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any Muslims and Croats -- or how many of them were there? Because you said that there were some Muslims and Croats who returned or who stayed in this area throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the war there were Muslim and Croats who remained in Ilidza and they live there to this day. I don't know if this Court has this information from 1994 from IFOR or UNHCR to the effect that a massive number of Muslims remained in Ilidza living there throughout the war and they still reside there to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many Muslims did you convert to Christianity in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. Are you trying to say whether we put pressure on them to convert to the Orthodox faith? Well, that's really absurd. Everyone is free to choose what job they will do, what religion they will abide by. So that was never in our plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's "van svijke pomitaj" [phoen], I wouldn't really say "observed." I would say "out of mind." Well, the reason I'm asking you this is because of what Prstojevic quoted.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO CEKLIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, that's just sheer rhetoric, as I -- it had nothing to do with reality. It was very far from reality nor there was ever anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ceklic. I have no further questions. Thank you for coming to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Ceklic. On behalf the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you. May I just put a question here if you allow me to the President of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We do not entertain a question from the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's of a private nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to go to private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's of a private nature. No, no. If I may just exchange greetings with Mr. President -- with the President before I leave The Hague Tribunal, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Cekic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies. His name was Ceklic, not Cekic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is really admirable how well you can actually pronounce our last names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tesic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Tesic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule that we have here at the -- at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E) of Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that may amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. However, in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in -- under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Tesic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tesic. Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you for pausing between my question and your answer, because we have to wait for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now 1D7198, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see the statement of yours on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page with his signature on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately reflect your words, what you've said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today that were put to you on that occasion, would your answer in essence be the same?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, in essence they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement under 92 ter, Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not tendering any associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note, Mr. Robinson, Mr. Karadzic, that it has been the -- our practice that when a substantial new information is added to the statement less than 48 hours prior to testimony, that new information should be led live. Do you have any observation in that regard? I'm referring to the last four paragraphs relating to the adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we don't -- we didn't -- first of all, we did run a little short of the 48-hour requirement, and if I -- I was expecting if the Prosecution had any problem with that we would have rescheduled the witness, and it would be our preference not to lead those live, and we also don't think they're particularly substantial, but if the Chamber -- whenever you want to hear something live, of course, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the circumstances, particularly in which the Prosecution does not oppose the admission, on an exceptional basis we'll admit the statement in its entirety, but we are making sure that we are not deviating from our practice. Please bear that in mind in the future. Yes. We'll receive the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3115, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out a short summary statement by Mr. Branimir Tesic in English. [In English] Branimir Tesic was born on 6th of May, 1995, in Bratunac, and currently resides in Ljubovija Serbia. In 1992, he was appointed as the deputy commander of a Serbian police station in Bratunac. The Bratunac SJB employed mainly Muslims but also some Serbs. Interethnic relations were satisfactory until the beginning of the war as tensions mounted and people began obtaining weapons; however, people became concerned for their safety and began leaving Bratunac. In Bratunac in 1991, a large number of Muslims gathered in front of the municipality building in Bratunac where a small military police unit came from Tuzla to take over the card files. The Muslims refused to let them enter the building. After this news spread, Serbs started to gather in order to support the JNA. Thanks to the police who separated the people, large-scale incidents were prevented. Later, the commander of the military police unit was forced to order firing in the air in order to make the Muslims move away from the them, and then he withdrew with the unit. They moved into a primary school building near the municipality building while the Muslim police remained in the police building, so making two police stations on a grid-way. Later the Muslims left this police station with the other and handed over this police station to the Serbian police. Mr. Tesic and other policemen with an army unit were required to ask the inhabitants of the area who owned weapons illegally to hand over the weapons to the police station. In early May 1992, Branimir Tesic and a police patrol were assigned to escort a struck to Milici. On their way back, in Hranca, they saw shooting all around them and something was burning. They were told that Muslims had attacked a JNA column that was withdrawing from the Central Bosnia towards Serbia, and this was confirmed later when they returned to Bratunac. Branimir Tesic was not aware that some Muslims were brought to Bratunac from Hranca that evening and locked up at the Vuk Karadzic elementary school, nor did he know that some Muslims were killed during that time because he was not there nor he was -- nor was he needed to interfere. Regarding the operation in Glogova in early May 1992, Branimir Tesic had no specific knowledge because he was not there. Through later -- though later he knew that some vehicles which were carrying some Muslims, he did not know if any Muslims were taken to Vuk Karadzic elementary school on that day. Both army and civilian authorities had a lot of problems with volunteers. They were very hard to control, and many were often drunk or steal property. They even physically attacked policemen and the station itself. In late May 1992, Branimir Tesic heard rumours that Muslims in Sandici had ambushed a military armoured vehicle travelling from Bratunac to Vlasenica. That night, the chief of the police station, Milutin Milosevic, was captured and killed subsequently. Many soldiers were killed or wounded there. Later, they tried to exchange the bodies with the Muslims but were refused. Around 14th of July 1995, Branimir Tesic heard that Zeljko Ninkovic, a member of the PJP, was killed in Sandici during an attack launched by the Muslims from other police -- policemen who were with Ninkovic that day. About the incident in the buildings of the farmers cooperative in Kravica, Branimir Tesic heard that one of the Muslims started shooting at the police with a rifle and then the security officers opened fire -- fires on the Muslims. And that is a short summary. I don't have questions for this -- for witness for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Before we take the break, I was checking my records concerning the notification for this witness, and I was wondering if the Chamber could also check, because my records show that we provided 59 hours notice, but perhaps you could check your own records. Maybe you didn't receive notice when I did, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a bit longer break than usual, for 35 minutes, and resume at 10 past 11.00. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to wait until after this, as I appreciate you didn't see me, but I would -- just wanted to say that the distinction between 48 hours, 50 hours, and so on may be a distinction without a difference depending upon the substance of the additional information. I think the Trial Chamber has made that clear, so I -- we've made the point before that it isn't necessarily a bright line test depending on the nature of the information provided, and I think the Court has made that clear too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay. The Judges' deliberation went a bit longer than expected. Yes, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tesic.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I would like to start by talking about the days after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995. At paragraph 37 of your statement, you said that one evening you saw a number of buses with Muslims arriving and staying in Bratunac overnight. The police was guarding the prisoners at night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: It is correct that the military police were guarding those prisoners during the night, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, let me briefly read you what Bogdan Subotic, a military policeman, said in the Popovic case on the 1st September 2008 at transcript 24991 and 24992. He's describing the military police escorting a column of buses from Nova Kasaba to Bratunac. And then he's asked: "Q. When you arrived in Bratunac, who did you hand the prisoners over, to whom and where? "A. I handed them over to members of the station of the interior in Bratunac, the civilian police. They awaited us at the entrance of the school." And later on he further explained: "Can you tell me more about it?" And he says: "I was at the head of the column. I reached the gate of the elementary school. I waited a member of the civilian police to come out, and then I informed them that I had POWs. He said - the police, the civilian police - that he was informed and said that he should move the armoured vehicle around so that the buses could enter into the school." So I'm asking you again, the civilian police was guarding the prisoners in Bratunac that night; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: No. The civilian police did not guard the prisoners during that night at Bratunac. First of all, you have just said that the civilian police had to move their armoured vehicles, but the civilian police never had any armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There must have been a misunderstanding. This is not what I said. This is the military policeman who testified and said that he was told to move their armoured vehicle in order to let the buses to enter the school. But you gave an interview to the office of the prosecutor of the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 2008, and in that context you -- you gave a slightly different answer to the similar question. You were asked: "Our information is that you instructed some policemen to go and help to secure the people." And your answer was: "That is possible. That's possible, but what I'm saying is that I was not in position -- in a position to give out or to assign any people to assist the security." So if I understand correctly what you said to the prosecutor in Bosnia is that it's possible that civilian police was there, but as far as you knew, you didn't give any order. You didn't deploy them, but it's possible that they were there. Is this your testimony today, or you change your position and now you're saying that the civilian police was not guarding the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: No, no. I have not changed my position. This isn't about positions but about what happened. It's possible that there was someone, but no order was issued. I didn't have enough staff at the Bratunac police station to provide security to buses carrying Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. So you agree that it's possible that the police was there. Now, in the same interview to the Prosecutor in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you also said that you only heard about the shooting and the killings that night at the Vuk Karadzic school and the stadium, and we are talking about 1995, that you only heard later through the trials. Now, you meant the trials here in The Hague, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both here in The Hague and the trials in Bosnia-Herzegovina, before the court of BH. I heard shooting, but at that time you could hear shouting all about the place, from the stadium, from the school, from the Poca Usa [phoen], from Srebrenica, from Voljavica. You could hear shooting from all over the place at the time. And we learned of the killings only later when the buildings, the schools, and so on, were vacated and the civilian protection entered and found a number of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So what you said at paragraph 37 of your statement is not accurate, because -- and I read, you say: "I do not know if there was shooting in the town that night and if any Muslim were killed."

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Not that night. I didn't know whether anybody was killed that night, but later we learned that people had been killed, that is, dead bodies were discovered, bodies of people who had probably been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: All right. So you learned later through the trials as you explained a few seconds ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, can I have P04398, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Tesic, this is an article that was published in "The Independent," an English newspaper, on the 21st of July 1995. So more or less a week after the 13 of July. And if we go to the first page at paragraph 3, it says: "One Serb woman who claimed to have seen the main execution site, a playground in Bratunac, spoke of a field knee-deep in blood. And the killings are said to be continuing. 'It is terrible what they are doing. If I could, I would call the people in Bratunac for this,' the woman said." And on the second page in paragraph 4: "The two women say that the killing were going on at the 'playground' earlier described as a stadium and a school near some kind of warehouse. Testimony from all other sources mention the same sites." So two random women from Serbia knew that people were killed at that time and you, the deputy commander of the police, that probably, as you said, but it was in fact there guarding the prisoners, you only heard about this event through the trials in The Hague or before the Bosnian Serb court. Is this your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying that I first learned of this in The Hague. The information reached me much sooner when the buildings -- the school buildings were vacated. Then the news spread. But what I'm trying to say, that the civilian police of Bratunac was not charged with guarding those buses. At the time, we didn't have enough staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: -- because they were in the field, and we could not assign anyone to securing these buses. We merely secured roads from Bratunac to Kravica, Konjevic Polje, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you were a deputy commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- a question was put to the witness as if he hadn't answered at the top of page 42. He said that they learned as soon as the school was vacated, that they learned of the killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: If I may answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Let's proceed, Mr. Costi, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you said at paragraph 39 that Zeljko Ninkovic was killed in the evening of the 13th July. In fact, he was killed early in the morning of the 13th July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Here in paragraph 39 it says the 14th of July, 1995, but I reiterate that I do not remember the exact date. It was during that period, however. He was a police officer of the Bratunac police station. At that moment he had been -- he was part of the unit from Zvornik and that unit that secured that the road probably from Kravica to Konjevic Polje. This officer, Zeljko Ninkovic, was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me just clarify: At paragraph 39 you said that on the 14th you learned that the evening before, meaning the 13th, Ninkovic was killed. So it's not the 14th, the date you indicated in your statement, but I -- I understand your testimony. You're not sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can I have P06189, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, if we see the document on the screen, at the -- it says that in the early morning hours of the 13th July 1995, the 1st PJP Company Zvornik SJB had contact with a large enemy group. And it goes on and it says: "However, Zeljko Ninkovic, a policeman from the 1st Company, born in 1967, was killed." So this report, CJB report, Zvornik CJB report indicates that he was killed in the morning, early hours at 4.00 in the morning of the 13th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Don't ask me if this is correct. If such a document was drafted and sent out, it's probably true. This document bears the date of 13 July and probably it is accurate. You're asking me after 20-odd years if I remember the date or possibly the hour when someone was killed. I can't know that now. I can't know the exact hour when someone was killed. This is a dispatch and there is no signature on it, but it says that it was -- the original was signed by Dragomir Vasic, and I think it must be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well. So -- and the funeral of Ninkovic was the day after, on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Probably on the day after he was killed in accordance to Serbian customs -- not only Serbian customs. There must -- a certain time must elapse before someone was buried. So he was probably buried on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. At paragraph 40 of your statement you say that you heard later about the massacre at the Kravica warehouse. Now, you actually heard about it on the 14th, didn't you? So only a few hours after people were killed at the Kravica warehouse, because on the 14th in Bratunac, everyone was talking about it; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: I cannot say if I learned of it on the 14th, but probably at the moment when it was happening I was in no position to know about it. I was at Bratunac and they were at Sandici, which is some 13 or 14 kilometres away. A certain time had to pass, a few hours at the least, for the news to spread that the people were being killed there. But I was nowhere close to Sandici on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well. So let's go back in time to 1992. In your statement at paragraph 27 and 28, you said that you only heard later that Muslims were kept at the football stadium, and that you only heard later that Muslims were detained and some of them killed at the Vuk Karadzic school. We're talking about May 1992; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Here in my statement it says later. "Later" can mean anything, a few hours later or ten days later. When people gathered at the stadium, I probably knew a few hours later that this was happening. The Muslim population came there mostly voluntarily or escorted -- or rather, secured by the TO. Our orders were not to interfere with the TO's business, and they were part of the armed forces, the JNA. Besides the TO, there was a small JNA unit present, and they had their own military police squad. Apart from the Bratunac MP, there was also this military unit of the JNA, and we had received orders by Chief Milutin Milosevic who, as far as we knew, had been in touch with the then CJB of the Birca Romanija district, and we were ordered not to interfere with what the TO and the army were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well then. You said this in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we have P04308. And if we can please go to the last page, page 282.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So this that you should have in front of you, it's an aerial picture of Bratunac that you can probably recognise. Now, you can see, can't you, the -- that -- okay. Sorry. Now I can finally see it in front of my screen. Apologies. You can see that -- what is the stadium, can't you, is on the left side, is this empty field close to where we have the labour "Vuk Karadzic school"; right? That's the stadium; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you can also see the Vuk Karadzic school itself because it's pointed with a red arrow, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you can also see the police station is indicated right in the centre of this picture.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
