utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that this is not more than a five-minute walk from the police station to the Vuk Karadzic school and the stadium? So my question for you is: No matter what you were ordered or not, you must have known at the time what was going on at the stadium and the school? You must have known as deputy head of the police that thousands of Muslims were brought there, right, and not later.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: It is correct that this is within five minutes walking, but if you're saying that I had to know, no, I didn't. Why should I have to know. I know that Muslims are gathering on the stadium, the football pitch, and that's what I stated in an earlier statement. We didn't provide security to them, and I don't see why I had to know. Well, yes, I did know that they were gathering there. The Muslims were gathering at the football pitch of Bratunac on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Before we move on, so you did know that the Muslims were at the football stadium and the Vuk Karadzic school at the time they were there and not later as you said in your statement.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: I knew that these Muslims were gathering at the football pitch, and later we learned about some events, that there had been victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have 65 ter 24757A.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Tesic, this is a statement that B1070, a protected witness in the Slobodan Milosevic, gave again to the BiH MUP, this time on the 29th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And if we go to e-court pages 8 and 9 of the English and B/C/S 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And again the witness described --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page in English version. Sorry. It starts about -- yeah, around 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So the witness says he was again detained at the stadium and then brought to the Vuk Karadzic school, and he says when he was still in the stadium. "At around 1900 hours, the residents were ordered to form two lines and start walking towards the entrance gate of the stadium where there were guards. There was a number of special task forces from Belgrade at the gate separating men aged between 15 and 50 from women, children, and old men who were led towards the trucks parked in front of Lamela in Bratunac. Once he finished separating us, we were lined up in four rows. At that moment, Miroslav Deronjic, chairman of the SDS of Bratunac, Rodoljub Djukanovic, known as Rocko, chairman of the Executive Board of the Bratunac Municipal Assembly, Branimir Tesic known as Baka, deputy commander of the Serbian police station in Bratunac came by." Now, we can see from this statement that the process of boarding women and children on the trucks to be brought outside Bratunac and bringing the men to the Vuk Karadzic school happened at the same time. Now, you said that you might have been present when women and children were boarded on buses. I'm asking you did you also witness men selected and walked to the close by Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: As a said a while ago and as I said in my statement, I may have been near the stadium when the Muslim population were being assembled there. I didn't specify women or children. There were men there boarding the buses. Most probably, again I must point out I don't quite remember, we provided police escort, military police specifically. We entrusted them with the buses, and they were off to Kladanj. As I said a while ago I was not a deputy head. I was deputy commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So how do you explain the two witnesses saw you there before being brought to the Vuk Karadzic school? Both these witnesses we discussed were then brought to the Vuk Karadzic school, not on a bus or nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: As I said, I don't remember. I don't know that they were taken there in my presence. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to discuss the events of the 9th of May in Glogova. You said in your statement at paragraph 25 that you know nothing specific about it. However, the police was involved, wasn't it, in the operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So this Chamber heard the evidence of Milenko Katanic, and it is his statement at P04374, at paragraph 35, he said -- and Milenko Katanic took part to this operation: "I was asked about the units involved in the operation. I mentioned Captain Reljic from Novi Sad Corps. The police, public security station also had their armed forces. They were also deployed and they all had their assignments." So I'm asking again, the police was indeed involved in the operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: I categorically assert that the police were not involved in this operation. This witness is not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well. We'll let the Trial Chamber to decide who is telling the truth. And then the goal of the operation. You said that the operation was aimed to -- to take weapons illegally detained. Now, you might know that Miroslav Deronjic pled guilty to crimes against humanity for the killings of 64 Bosnian Muslim civilian in Glogova, the forcible displacement of the rest of the population, and the destruction of religious and civilian property in Glogova. I'm asking you, the operation was not to disarm the population, was it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Based on my information, based on what I heard, the objective was to do something about the communication between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje, to make it safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, again, Milenko Katanic in the statement mentioned before at part -- at P4374 at paragraph 38, says: "I've been told that what Deronjic said and pled guilty to, is that the purpose to the Glogova operation was to remove the Muslim population of Glogova from Bratunac municipality." And then he said: "That is the conclusion I myself made after the operation, but that is not something I knew during the operation." So I'm asking you: Would you agree with Mr. Katanic that the conclusion you should reach today is that the operation was not to disarm or to secure the road, but it was, in fact, to expel the population?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree. Milenko Katanic was a close associate of Miroslav Deronjic, and he was probably in a better position than me to know. I didn't know. I wasn't privy to that kind of information, and I was not involved in politics. I was not even involved in any preparations, actions, or anything at all that took place there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: As you said, Milenko Katanic was in a better position than you to assess. So you're not willing to change your view today in light of what a person that was better positioned than you said?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Why would I? I believed -- what I believed at the time, and I still believe the same thing: Milenko Katanic is entitled to his own views and he may have known better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at paragraph 30 of your statement, you said you had problems with the volunteers and you describe it further in additional paragraph that were add to your statement. What you didn't say is that the Serbs' authorities started being concerned with the problem with the volunteers only when they start attacking Serbs' houses. Isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: The Serb authorities were concerned right after certain steps were taken by the volunteers against the Muslim population. It wasn't just later when they actually started attacking Serb homes. The municipal authorities reached certain conclusions and took certain decisions to drive out the paramilitary units. Nevertheless, at the time they did not have sufficient manpower to achieve that and to drive the units out of the Bratunac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 04695, please. And page 2 and 3 of the English version and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Tesic, this is a report of a performance inspection that was made on the 22nd and 23rd of August, 1993, at the Bratunac SJB. They discuss several issues, and if we look at the last paragraph in the English version of this page, we see there's after all this talk which were held at Bratunac SJB, we had a meeting with representative of all, say, the Bratunac Serb authorities, the army, the president of the municipality, the chairman -- chairman of the SDS, Zoran Tesic on behalf of the municipality, other representative of the army, the head of the SJB Luka Bogdanovic, the commander Ljubomir Borovcanin, the deputy chief Branimir Tesic. And now probably the translation should have said "deputy commander," as you specified before. "Now, during this meeting, the SJB chief gave a short overview," and I'm reading, "on the activities of the Bratunac SJB from the beginning of the war until today," so August 1992, "saying that four SJB member lost their lives in this war so far, the chief and three service police officers. He stated further," and this is the relevant part, "that they have problems with different volunteer units on their territory which in the beginning of the war played a role in the war but which later on got mainly involved in robberies and trouble making on the territory of the municipality." Further down on page 2, almost at the bottom, and page 3 of the B/C/S, then there are conclusion by the president of the municipality, Simic. He talks about problems in the organisation, and then he talks about: "A lot has been done already." And that: "The police should be engaged especially in preventing of further lootings because Serbian houses are now being looted too." So my understanding of this document is that the Serb authorities played a role -- sorry, the Serb authorities' view is that the volunteers played a role at the beginning of the war, but then at one point it was necessary to take steps, because also Serbian houses were looted. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: May I just know the date of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I believe it happened between the 22nd and 23rd of August, 1992, because this is a report of this inspection that took place in these two days. So either one of the two. The report doesn't specify which day.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: You're asking me about some things that you probably got from Mr. Luka Bogdanovic's contribution. These are his words. That was the way he phrased it. I have no idea about the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown who authored or produced this report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: It's on the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But do you agree you were at the meeting, Mr. Tesic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I could agree if that's what the document shows. I don't particularly remember, and it's very difficult for me to say anything. I see that the report was submitted by Blagoje Sasa. I have no idea who that person is, Sasa Blagojevic. Perhaps we could find some information in the header. Who was this produced by? A centre, a security centre. I have no idea who this person is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Sarajevo CSB. Shall we show him the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The header reads: "The Birac Romanija Centre," and the police station was formally under that centre. Nonetheless, I did not know a person named Sasa Blagojevic, which doesn't mean that there wasn't a person named that around. Perhaps he was there and attended the meeting. I trust the document, but I can't remember the specific meeting held sometime in August back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Tesic, was a -- what I'm asking you is whether you agree with what I said, which is that the volunteers were useful, were used at the beginning -- they had a role at the beginning of the war and that you started being concerned with the lootings only when they start attacking Serbs' houses?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: They never did us any good, not even back at the outset. They always stirred trouble. Therefore, I would not agree with the words stated here by the then commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we go now to the paragraph 10 of the same document, which is at page 4 of the English version and page -- sorry. My mistake. Not paragraph 10 but is page 2 of the English version and B/C/S page 1, at the bottom. And -- exactly. That's the paragraph I'm interested for the English. The one that begin -- there's a paragraph at the beginning that talks about investigation of war crimes and should be the last paragraph of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And the English version says: "In proving of war crimes and identifying of war criminals, the Bratunac SJB had achieved significant results using all available means and all operative knowledge based on which they created a photo and video documentation of the victims of the genocide while they are compiling a list of perpetrators of Muslim nationality who carried out the genocide against the Serbian nation based on the civil records, that is to say personal IDs, which they have been able to keep in safe custody of the SJB." Now, as head commander of the Bratunac SJB, isn't it true that you achieved significant result investigating war crimes by the Muslims, but I don't see mention of any investigation on possible war crimes committed by the Serbs, for example, at the Vuk Karadzic school, just two or three months before? Isn't it true that the document doesn't mention any investigation of Serb crimes, war crimes?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: As for any war crimes investigations conducted by the then public security station in Bratunac, this was something that was down to the crime police, the inspectors working there, in co-operation with the people from the Birac Romanija region while I was the deputy commander. This wasn't my job. And whatever they eventually achieved was not available to me. They submitted reports only to the chief of what used to be the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you don't recall any investigation on war crimes potentially committed by the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: I didn't really go into investigations conducted by different service, that of the centre or that of the public security station. Again, I was deputy commander, and I was working at a police station. I had no jurisdiction at all over the work of the crime police at the Bratunac public security station or indeed the public security centre police.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we have in document admitted, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6196.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, can I have 65 ter 18496. And here it's e-court page 4 for the English and 3 for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, this is another report of a similar inspection, this time in September 1992, and paragraph 10 at page 4 of the English says again: "As for the documenting of war crimes against the Serbian people committed by Muslim extremists, 46 cases were documented." So again, no mention of any investigation on possible war crimes committed by the Serb authorities, again like at the Vuk Karadzic school or Glogova, nothing like that; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Again you talk about the Serb authorities committing crimes. This is not something that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: This report is probably accurate, and it was probably put together by a control team that visited the Bratunac Public Security Station, but I would like to know who signed it, who produced it, and when exactly that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yes, signed by the inspector for police duties and tasks and reported, and again -- reported again as the one we saw before to Sarajevo Romanija. Now, if we could now look at paragraph 6 of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And it's e-court page 3 for both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: It says: "The paramilitary formation in the area of Bratunac SJB from among the civilian berets, 50 men in total, of which 30 are locals, whereas 20 of them are from the Republic of Serbia, the public security station is engaged with its own forces and with assistance of the military and the civilian authorities in the dispersal of such formation in order to put them under the command of the armed forces of Republika Srpska." So if I'm not wrong, far from investigating crime possibly committed by these formations, you were actually busy to try to put them under the control of the VRS; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: This is an entirely different paramilitary unit who you're talking about here at paragraph 6. We are looking at a unit here which arrived in the area I think back in 1993. The unit was led --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: The document is from 1992, so we are not talking about a unit that entered in the area one year later the report -- after the report.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: The one thing that's confusing me is it reads here that the unit numbered 20 men from the RS and about 30 locals, and the only unit I know of that was around which corresponds with this description was in 1993 and it was led by an officer from Serbia, actually from Montenegro, Vasilije Mijovic, who brought over a number of men from Serbia and put together about 30 locals and then performed some specialised training with these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. We have very little time. My question wasn't who are these men but whether no steps was taken to investigate these people. Rather, the point was to take them under control without any investigation as whether war crimes were committed. These units that you said you tried to ...

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 we're not talking about paramilitary units that committed crimes early in 1992. We're talking about an entirely paramilitary unit here. We did run into trouble with this one as well. This particular paramilitary unit attacked a police station and wounded one of our police officers. Members of this paramilitary unit were terrorising ethnic Serbs as well. Well-regarded citizens of Bratunac who were being brought in on account of allegedly committing crimes. They would interrogate them, beat them up, take them off somewhere to Serbia and lock them up there. The Bratunac police station actually had an armed clash with these units. One of our police officers was even wounded during that clash. And then the RS authorities somehow managed to get these men out of Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can I admit this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me now briefly move back in 1995, July 1995. Paragraph 36 of your statement you said you went to Potocari after the fall of Srebrenica, and you went with a policeman called Dragan Neskovic. In Potocari, you witnessed a woman and children being loaded onto the buses. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I went there with this police officer Dragan Neskovic, but I did not see any women or children there. There were elderly persons being loaded onto buses there and able-bodied men, but I only caught the very start of this process of people being loaded on the buses. I was only there for a very brief while for certain reasons which I will not go into now.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: We know the reason. Let me now -- this is not what you actually said in your interview with the Prosecutor at the state court of Bosnia-Hercegovina. What you said is that: "The first time I saw people, women and children, getting onto the buses was in Potocari." So you did see not just elderly men but also women and children being loaded on the buses, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: I can assert now that I'm certain that I saw elderly men and able-bodied men boarding the buses, but that was at the very start, the early stage, the first couple of buses. I stayed no more than half an hour in Potocari before I went back to the station, which was in the first day when the Muslim population reached Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, people were asking for help, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: What people do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: People that were pushed and loaded on the buses. Prisoners -- I mean, sorry, refugees in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear anyone asking for help because I was there at the very start, and I didn't see that anyone was pushing anyone onto the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me read you what Dragan Neskovic, the policeman you went with, testified in the Popovic case on the 28th of October, 2008, at transcript 27431. "I probably would have stayed longer, but many people knew me. They were calling my name. I couldn't bear that. I could not help everybody. I could not even maybe help the two that I was looking for. It would have been hard to do. It was war. So I returned, and Tesic stayed behind." Now, Neskovic returned to Bratunac because he could not bear the fact that people were asking for help. But you don't recall anyone begging for help, although you stayed behind. Is this your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: No. I arrived there with Neskovic, and I went back to the police station with Neskovic. Now, when we arrived at Potocari, he went one way and I went another way. We went through the mass of people there and probably Neskovic was better known by those people than I was because he was older than I was and he had worked there longer in that service, and these were all people from the Srebrenica municipality who didn't really know me too well. So when I went and walked amongst those people, I questioned them. I asked them a bit about what was going on there, and he wasn't there, but we returned -- I returned to the police station with Neskovic in the same police car.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Thank you. I hope I will be brief and complete this soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tesic, where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Now as 20 and something years before, I lived in -- I live in Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you tell the Trial Chamber how far Ljubovija is from Bratunac as the crow flies and also if you go by road.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, if you take the road it's about 7 to 8 kilometres, but as the crow flies it's about 3 kilometres perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you spend your time when you were not on duty, and where did you spend your nights?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Whenever I wasn't on duty I was at home in Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see -- or, rather, on page 52 the Prosecutor was trying to establish when exactly you arrived there and what you saw.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 24757, please. That is a statement that -- I believe page 10 in the Serbian language and pages 8 and 9 in the English. But it's sufficient to have the Serbian version on the screen. As for the other participants here, they can follow it on page 8 and 9. It doesn't have to be broadcast, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have a redacted version, and we'll broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just zoom in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you didn't see people being separated; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's see what we can read here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in a bit. This is really not -- it's a bit difficult to read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Once the separation was complete, they were lined up in fours, and at the -- at that point in time, Deronjic, Djukanovic, and Tesic arrived, and they -- towards the end of the column. Now, is this consistent with what you know, that actually you arrived there once the separation had already been complete?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said before that it is possible that I was near the stadium, in the vicinity somewhere, when the Muslim population -- when the Muslim civilians were entering the buses to be transported, but I can't really recall the details. We probably provide the military -- police escort to assist the -- in the transport of these men towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The point that I'm trying to ask you about is this: The Prosecutor showed you this statement trying to show, to prove that you were there while the separation was going on and that you saw it, but here in the statement it says that you arrived there after the separation was already done. So which is true, what you've said and what we see or what the Prosecutor claimed?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say again I did not see anyone being separated at that time, nor did I see anyone already having been separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although the witness has answered it, the question was very much leading. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I was just trying to make a point to show, namely, that the statement doesn't really differ from this witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 54, from lines 15 and on, there is talk about various militaries. Now, first let me ask you a general question. What was the position of the authorities towards the various military groups, and has it changed and at what point?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, the authorities were never quite receptive of the paramilitary units. As I've said before, they took the decision not at the time where we saw that document in August or September. Decisions to that effect were taken much earlier, in April or May. The authorities' position was that paramilitary formations and units should be expelled. However, these paramilitary units had the support of the population. There was a large rally of citizens from Bratunac and refugees from Srebrenica, Serbs, because all the villages around Srebrenica had been torched and destroyed. So these people rallied there outside the municipal building and they did not allow -- or, rather, they expressed their support of the paramilitary units. So most of these people were refugees from these villages that had been at that time in May and June already torched and people expelled from them by Muslim extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 747, 65 ter 747 in e-court. Could we also see English, because it's more legible. Could we see the last -- the next page, please -- rather, the next two pages. This is just the cover page. Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serbian version is rather difficult to read out, so I will read it out in English. "[In English] Serbian Republic of BH, SAO of Birac, Bratunac municipality Crisis Staff, Bratunac, 6th of May, 1992. "On the basis of the Decision of the National Security Council of the Serbian Republic of BH and pursuant to the SAO Birac Crisis Staff Decision and the Decision of the commissioner of the government of the Serbian Republic of BH for the Birac area, the Bratunac municipality Crisis Staff hereby takes the following decision: All paramilitary formations should leave the territory of Bratunac by 1600 hours on 7th of May 1992. "The Decision was taken unanimously. "If the paramilitary formations fail to act on the Decision, legal military formations will be ordered to implement it." [Interpretation] How does this tally with what you knew about the position that the authorities took vis-a-vis the paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, here we can see that the municipal authorities adopted this kind of decision already in early May. In other words, paramilitary formations were never well received as far as the authorities and the police were concerned. However, there you had it. These crimes had occurred in the area of the Srebrenica municipality in Serbs villages, but also in Serb villages in the Bratunac municipality where hundreds and thousands of citizens had moved in order -- because their villages -- had moved to because their villages had been torched and destroyed. And they supported these are paramilitary formations which, of course, was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber needs to rise at the moment. We'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll discuss it after the break. We'll resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I would like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3116, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could would now take a look at 00748 on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tesic, the document of the 6th of May that we just saw a moment ago, it was obviously put out before -- or, rather, let me put it this way: When did Judge Zekic die? When was he killed?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Mr. Goran Zekic was killed on the 7th of May, 1992. On his way back from Srebrenica to Bratunac he was taking a roundabout way and this was close to Zalazje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he killed in fighting or was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't killed in combat. He was a civilian. He was deputy in the pre-war BH Assembly, and after the war that was the Serbian Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was in a civilian vehicle, and an acquaintance of his, Delivoje Sorak, was also in the car with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was he a judge?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: He was a judge in the then Lower Court in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I think -- I thought he might have been the president of the court as well, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise the signature that you see now?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: This is the signature of Zoran Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to tell you this, although it's more legible in English. On the 1st of May, there is a reference to a decision by the National Security Council of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Birac Crisis Staff, and it says that an order is being issued forbidding all paramilitary formations and illegal citizens to operate in the territory of Bratunac municipality. So an order forbidding all paramilitary formations and illegal citizens to operate in the territory of Bratunac municipality. All paramilitary formations and illegal citizens as well as all groups that have come in from outside are hereby forbidden to operate in the territory of the municipality. The only authorised units that can operate in military terms are in the territory of -- in other words, only JNA, Yugoslav People's Army units, and TO defence units of the Serbian Republic have the right to deal with military issues and performing duties in the state of war that has been declared in the territory of Bratunac municipality. Now, have you received this order?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests that the witness repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Tesic. Interpreters couldn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that the police station ever received this order -- or, rather, the public security station in Bratunac. I can't see -- because I see here that it says inform the TO -- the TO headquarters and the Bratunac Public Security Station of this order, but I don't see that it was actually forwarded to the public security station in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But were you aware, did you know that this was the position of the authorities vis-a-vis paramilitary units even before the -- they began mistreating Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know of this position and decisions to that effect that were taken by the Crisis Staff in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I -- I would like to tender this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3117, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now briefly take a look at P1696. That was a document that was just admitted into evidence a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often did these inspections visit you at the public security station? How often did they go there?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't really say that they came often. Based on the reports you can conclude that this was probably quarterly, on a quarterly basis, every two or three months, or, rather, when there was a problem, then they would come.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this is not the same document, 04695 on the 65 ter list, and the P, that was 6196. 6196, not 16. Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in this report we see that it was of the 27th of August, and it says in line 5 or 6 that there is no crime scene technician. Now, did you have a crime scene technician at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: At the time -- let me just try and -- and remember that. I'm sorry. I need to jog my memory. No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please look at the third bullet. When examining the documents of the crime service at this public security station, I established that there is a lot of documented information on perpetrators of crimes. Did you collect documents only -- gather information only on Muslim perpetrators or how did you do that work?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've said a few moments ago answering Mr. Prosecutor's questions, the job of documenting crimes, war crimes, was done by members of the crime prevention service in co-operation with the crime prevention service of the public security centre of the Birac-Romanija area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you may be aware of this. It says here that the authorities were not -- had not yet been -- the judicial organs have not yet been established, so they're transferred to the Lower Court in Zvornik. So are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, there was never a judicial organ in Bratunac, not during the war. The competent court was the Lower Court in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see the third page, please. It says at the top the commander of the police station then took the floor and he proposed that meetings should be held every day at this level, and also in order to resolve the problem of volunteers he proposed that all persons who were illegally in the territory of the Republika Srpska should be expelled and that lists of such persons should be compiled so that they would be forbidden and prevented from coming into Bratunac. Were you aware of this position?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And a little lower it says the president of the municipality, Ljubisav Simic, pointed out that there were numerous problems in organising all three levels of authorities in this area saying in the process that there were even members of the public security service who engaged in illicit acts and he asked that they be purged, and he also acknowledged that already a lot had been done in that area. Now, were you aware that there was this purge on -- going on within the security service organs and that this was the position of the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object this line of questioning which seems to me leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's very difficult to intervene when there's no pause at all. The witness has answered the question, but bear that in mind, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tesic, let me rephrase that. Was this position by the president of the municipality, Mr. Simic, implemented?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was implemented even from before. In the month of June there was a purge at the police station in Bratunac, and at that point the number of police officers was reduced, those who breached the discipline in any manner or committed some disciplinary infraction. Such policemen were dismissed. And we also reduced the number of police officers for the need of the Bratunac Battalion that existed at the time, and we sent some policemen at the request of the army to the ranks of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what was the situation with the communications at the time, and how was communication conducted with higher authorities, superior authorities?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, we did not always have telephone lines available. They weren't always functioning. So I think we used the military system, the military signal system, in order to be in touch with the Serb -- with Serbia, although we did use the radio station for some major issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tesic, would you put a pause before you start answering the question. And, Mr. Karadzic, how does this arise from the cross-examination at all?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was put to the witness, and it was proposed by the Prosecution with this witness, and of course the Prosecutor selected the portions that he asked the witness about, but there is a lot more that was not explored. It was very selective. Now, on the first page in the third paragraph it says that all the communications are down and they were requesting that some form of communication be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it does not mean that it opened every issue, but how is it relevant to the issue that you would like to raise or that was raised by Mr. Costi? Yes, Mr. Costi, you would like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Not really, Your Honours. The point was exactly the same. I mean, even if the document covers other issue, that doesn't open the door to touch it if it weren't discussed in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just point out that when document is admitted, you're admitting it for all purposes, so it seems logical that we would have a chance to explore areas in that document regardless of whether it arose from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is split, but the Chamber orders the accused to move on, Judge Baird dissenting, but my point is that there is no need to cover this issue repeatedly. Move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It would be much easier for the Defence if we knew the Chamber's position so we could reduce the Defence. Could we please see P1697.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, not 16 but 61.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6197.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many police officers did you have? A couple of minutes ago you said that you gave them all to the army. So how many did you have, and was the number sufficient for keeping law and order?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Once we had ceded a number of officers to the army, we were left with 20 something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This audit was done ten days after the previous one, and it says under item 1 that the station has a total of 24 police officers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat your question, the last part of your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph we read that they only had a fix -- fixed HF radio station for communication, and for telephones they only had local phones. Now, how does that tally with what Mr. Tesic is claiming?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. We only had local communications, communication lines, and the police had a couple of hand-held radio stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think that's the same issue. Unless -- unless he's linking the passage he's reading to something that arise from cross-examination, then that will be fine, but this seems to be purely question about communication system that are not related not only to my cross but to his testimony itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. You know the ruling.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Excellency, but if this police station is expected to control an area and inform the higher ranking bodies, we must establish whether that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry again, but of course this wasn't an issue in my cross whether they could actually perform investigation or whether they could communicate the result to higher-rank level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was covered in the cross-examination. Did you document and file criminal charges, and was a distinction made based on ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: Criminal reports were filed. There was no distinction made based on ethnic affiliation at the time when the station had been established and when we started functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 44, second subparagraph, we say -- we read that the police officers in the previous period have submitted 30 official notes that point to the existence of criminal -- criminal offences. Which service was in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Just one little point. The -- I never touched upon the issue of common crimes. I was talking about war crimes. So I don't know whether this arose and whether it is relevant at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit difficult to exclude the relevance of any criminal investigation. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please finish your answer. Who did this, and then I will have no further questions. What does this phrase "police officers" mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: "Police officers," this phrase refers to uniformed police officers of the Bratunac station, and in their work in the field they obtained operative intelligence, and based on that they drafted their official notes. These are submitted to the commander of the police station of Bratunac who then forwards it to the chief -- or, rather, informs the chief, and these notes are forwarded to the crime investigation service, and if they think it is of interest to the police station of Bratunac, then they inform them, but if it's about a criminal offence with a more serious sentence, then it is also forwarded to the CJB or the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question, Mr. Tesic. Did the Bratunac authorities take part in or contribute to the commission of war crimes such as the persecution of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR TESIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for calling me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have a question directed to the parties rather than to the witness, but I will do it while he's here. Shall we upload Exhibit D1 -- I'm sorry, Exhibit D3117. That's a report, a decision of Bratunac Crisis Staff, probably page 3 in English. Yes. It reads: "On the basis of the decision of the National Security Council of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on declaring an imminent threat of war and pursuant to the SAO Birac Crisis Staff Decision on declaring a state of emergency ..." And we also so similar phrases from the witness statement of previous one, Mr. Ceklic, paragraph 19 and 28, where he referred to the declaration of imminent threat of war and declaration of war -- or state of war in Ilidza municipality. So my question for the parties, Mr. Tieger or Mr. Karadzic, do we have any documentary evidence of a municipality declaring a state of war or imminent threat of war and whether it was for the municipality or the central government, i.e., to declare such things? Or if Mr. Tesic is capable of assisting us, could you tell us if you could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I can help you with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Excellency. We have seen the Law on All People's Defence and social self-protection. The municipality has the same powers in the area of all people's defence as the state. The president of the municipality is the Supreme Commander, and they have the right and the duty to make their own assessment when there's a threat. We later changed that, but it was taken over from Tito's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So -- yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Mr. President, I don't think we'll -- we have seen any references to the declaration of a state of war in a municipality prior to the decision referred to at the republic level in mid-April, and I similarly don't recall indications of the existence of state of imminent threat of war in a municipality that does not reference the republic-level decision, but that at the moment is based on my immediate recollection. We'll keep an eye on it with the Court's inquiry in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If the parties could provide the Chamber with references later on if they could. Very well. Mr. Tesic, that concludes your evidence, and on behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're bringing in the next witness, just to -- with respect to this next witness, this is actually a case where in fact the witness is testifying before the 48-hour period expires. I think perhaps the Chamber had this witness in mind instead of the previous one when it indicated that it was considering some paragraphs had to be led live. So we would hope that the same ruling would apply and that the four paragraphs in this statement could also be accepted without having been led live. The reason why the witness is testifying a little earlier than expected is because our expert witness, Dr. Pasalic, was sick, and he had to delay his arrival in The Hague by two days, and so instead of -- he arrived -- he was proofed yesterday. Instead of having him testify today, we moved this witness up in the order. So we apologise if it's an inconvenience to anyone and we hope that we'll be able to lead his evidence under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would leave it with Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On an exceptional basis, yes. But please bear that in mind. This will not be repeated. Were some paragraphs redacted from this witness's statement, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We've agreed to redact paragraphs 8 and 9 of the witness's statement, and we won't be offering the associated exhibit that was referenced in paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tesic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we are having two Mr. Tesics on the same day from Bratunac, Mr. Tesic. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Tesic, I must draw your attention to a particular Rule that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E) of Rules of Evidence and Procedure. Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something at that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that your answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except for the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Tesic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tesic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to pause between question and answer, and we should both speak slowly for everything to be recorded. Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D7195. Could we zoom in on the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read and sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us show the witness the last page for him to identify the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask the same questions to you live today, would your answers to those questions be essentially the same as the ones in the statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. In -- in general terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I seek to tender this statement under Rule 92 ter, and I will have another document that I will lead after dealing with the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3118, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out a short summary of Mr. Aleksandar Tesic's summary in English. [In English] Aleksandar Tesic was born on 23rd of January, 1954, in Bratunac BH. He lives in Ljubovija, Serbia. He was the secretary of the municipal Secretariat for National Defence in Bratunac. On one occasion a small unit of military police attempted to remove mobilisation records from the municipal building in Bratunac. A large group of Muslims gathered in front of the municipality building and more kept coming. Aleksandar Tesic, who was employed in national defence municipal secretariat, was asked to assist with the removal and believed that the SDA Muslim party was behind this gathering. The Muslims swore and hurled insulted at the army and Serbs and tried to confront physically the military police unit which had to fire into the air at one point. The police and military units were greatly outnumbered by the Muslims, and it was very likely that they would be physically attacked. Then the Serbs began to gather with the intention of protecting the police and the members of the JNA. Fortunately, in the end large conflicts were avoided. Regarding to the volunteers, Mr. Tesic said that they formed their open unit instead of referring to the police. They were hard to control, having lots of problems such as looting and being drunk often. They even attacked the police station. At a meeting of the Crisis Staff, Aleksandar Tesic learned that some volunteers took some Muslims to the Vuk Karadzic primary school. He said that what happened were -- there was a shock to them, and they all condemned it. After this, the Crisis Staff decided to disarm these volunteers and to expel them from Bratunac. One night the Crisis Staff decided to transport all the Muslims who were in the school because it was the only way to prevent an even worse disaster. On 9th of May, 1992, in order to prevent conflicts in Glogova, an operation to disarm the citizens were planned to be carried out. Later on, Aleksandar Tesic heard that some people were killed or you wounded. He mentioned that the atmosphere was charged with the previous night due to the killing of a judge -- of the judge Goran Zekic, a member of parliament who was killed by the Muslims in Srebrenica. He was told about the Muslim attack on the JNA convoy in Hranca on 2nd of May, 1992, and which had resulted in casualties. On one occasion he discovered the bodies of around 20 Muslims in the hangar. Later the bodies were buried, and he believed that the funeral of the dead Muslims were performed in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. He believed that the volunteers whom no one could control were responsible for the killing of the Muslims in Bratunac and Glogova. When General Mladic asked him about what to do to the people -- with the people in 1995, he assumed was referring to the Muslims in Srebrenica. He said that transport should be provided for those who wanted to leave. On 13th or 14th of July, 1995, he saw several buses loaded with Muslims in Bratunac. He did not hear the soldiers had abused anyone because no soldiers were in the city, nor did he hear anyone was killed. Few days later, he learned that from Ljupko Ilic that there were some Muslims corpse in the Vuk Karadzic primary school. He said that during the meetings of the Crisis Staff, he never heard President Radovan Karadzic issue any orders in connection with the persecution, imprisonment, or killing of the Muslims. Instead, the president always emphasised that they must adhere to the Geneva Conventions in relation to the Muslims and civilians. He thought that President Karadzic could not have known a single incident that took place in Bratunac during the war due to the lack of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Tesic, I would like to ask you a question about something that you state is your recollection of my stay in Bratunac. You talk about that in paragraph 43. What is your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to make one objection to the summary. Lines 14 on page 85: "He thought that President Karadzic could not have," there's a typo there, "heard of a single incident that took place in Bratunac during the war." That very strong statement was in a prior version of the witness's statement which was altered. So that summary does not now correctly reflect the last sentence of paragraph 42 which is what I think it goes to. So for the record, that is not in the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, the wording here is slightly different in that statement. It was probably an earlier summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We just noted that. As you know, your summary is not part of evidence, but please shall cautious in producing the summary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the question, or perhaps I should remind you. You describe your recollection of my visit when the convoy was stopped at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. It was late in 1992. There was a humanitarian convoy carrying food for Srebrenica. At the entry point to Bratunac, some grieving mothers stopped the convoy. Their close relatives had been killed in the fighting the previous summer, in autumn, and their villages had been burnt down. They stopped the convoy because they believed that the convoy would be benefiting their enemy, and they did not allow the convoy to go through. Nonetheless, President Karadzic had been informed by someone about this, so he travels to Bratunac. He addressed the people assembled there from the balcony of a building in Bratunac housing the Red Cross, saying that the civilians on the other side were not responsible for the crimes committed by their leaders and army, the Muslim army. He gave a speech about the role and importance of the Red Cross, saying that throughout its history, the Serb people have always complied with humanitarian law and the rights of their enemies, citing some examples from the Serb Bulgarian war in the late 19th century. This produced a result, meaning the convoy was allowed to get through carrying all of the goods that were en route for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What was the reaction of the assembled people to my words?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: People accepted, although with some difficulty and reluctance, what you said during that speech and as a result allowed the convoy through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What was the position take by the local authorities about the situation in which the convoy was stopped? Did they have a part in that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't specifically remember or indeed know what position was taken by each and every one of the people involved, but I don't think anyone stood up to oppose the president's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter 101189, please. That's my next document. Thank you. 01189, please. Are you familiar with this journal called "Nasa Rijec" and can you tell me exactly what it is?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, "Nasa Rijec" was a local newspaper in Bratunac. It mostly covered developments in the Podrinje area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is this piece called: "We are Building our own State." Is that article in reference to my visit that you describe in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know, nor indeed can I read what it says because the print is very, very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can zoom in on the upper right corner of the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: That will do, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you the following question: Towards the end of paragraph 2, is this a faithful reflection of my words: "We are building our own state, and we need to use our own behaviour to show the world that we deserve one. The best way for us to do this will be to show our enemies that we are not building our state by using our hatred towards them, because this is not in the spirit of the Serb people."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand fully what you mean. These are indeed your words. You often used these words in your speeches. I see the initials of the person who wrote this piece. It's probably Milan Jovanovic who was the editor-in-chief of the newspaper at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Next paragraph. "In front of an assembled crowd of citizens with mostly mothers, children, and fighters who had been killed there, as well as refugees from other areas..." When you previously talked about grieving mothers, are these the persons that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, the grieving mothers, the mothers of fighters who were killed and civilians who were killed, or perhaps also refugees. One thing that applied to all the Serb villages in Srebrenica municipality is -- Srebrenica municipality is that they were all set fire to, and the refugees were now in the Bratunac area where they were received. 1992 in particular, the fighting took a heavy toll. From the month of May, this situation went on through the summer and spilled over into 1993, late January, to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Towards the end of paragraph 1 it reads: "Karadzic told the assembled people that they should allow the convoy carrying humanitarian aid for Srebrenica's population through," and then they quote the example of the Serb-Bulgarian war. And the last thing it says: "When leaving the municipality, Karadzic met with the representatives of the convoy." Is this consistent with what you happened to know about my positions, those publicly expressed, and my positions on issues regarding humanitarian aid generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is perfectly consistent with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3119, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellency, at this point in time I have no further questions of Mr. Tesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have one issue that you would like to take up. Oh, fine, yes. That's fine. Mr. Tesic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case in most part has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's not your first time in the Tribunal; correct? You testified here as a Defence witness in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. April 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And told the truth in that testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I want to first ask you a little bit about your job during the wartime. You worked in civilian protection, which is part of the -- under the Ministry of Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I was not with civilian protection. Before the war from, the 1st of March, 1981, on, I worked with the secretariat for People's Defence in Bratunac in the service for observation, reporting information and early warning, command signals, and encryption, and then in 1992 specifically on the 2nd of May, unbeknownst to me and without me having submitted any request at all, the municipal Crisis Staff appointed me secretary of the secretariat for All People's Defence in Bratunac. Within the framework of the work done by that secretariat were also various tasks related to civilian protection. If you require further details on that, I'm talking about military records, so entering the information on military recruits, recruitment itself, and the persons being sent to perform their regular military term at a particular location. So all of this was registered and recorded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you and try to refer you to some of your prior testimony. The superior organ to the secretariat you worked in was in Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: At one point, yes, during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During the war. And above them was the headquarters in Pale; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: We didn't refer to it as headquarters. It was the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So the Ministry of Defence was above the Zvornik centre, which was above you. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And part -- let me just talk then about civil defence or civilian protection which you discussed in your prior testimony. This -- wait for the question. This is 65 ter 24746 at T7778 to 7780, your testimony in the Blagojevic case. You said -- the question was from Mr. Karnavas: "You indicated civil defence. Could you explain a little bit about what you meant by civil defence?" And your answer was: "Civil defence or civil protection is a separate segment of the defence and it is geared towards providing protection and safeguarding people, the inhabitants and the society's material resources." And then you go through the different aspects, which I won't go through, in detail, and then you said: "Then there was a unit for transport and supplies and a unit for sanitation for the terrain and a biological and chemical protection unit." So that was part of civilian defence in Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I remember well what I said, but I can tell you what I said at the time. I talked about the structure of the tasks performed by the secretariat for all people's defence in peacetime. However, there comes a time when mobilisation must be carried out of the municipal civilian protection staff. When that time comes, it can operate on an on-and-off basis, but it can also operate on a permanent basis, as in nonstop mobilisation. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: (redacted) - was appointed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait. We're in open session now, again, and I don't know what the witness is about to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you a question and try to speed this up. This is from your testimony in that same case. It's 78193. And what I'm getting to is that the municipal civilian protection staffs and the tasks of cleaning and sanitising the terrain were not under the command of the VRS. Do you agree with that? And I won't have to go through your testimony.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Civilian protection was a special body, a special department comprising a sanitation unit and clearly the terrain. The unit existed from before the war, but when the need arose, the unit was mobilised up to full complement, 100 per cent, and even extended. There was a platoon-level unit also numbering 33 men. The commander of that unit was Dragan Mirkovic who was the manager of the utilities, public utilities company in Bratunac. He was fully qualified to perform that job --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: -- because he had taken and completed a course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You've answered my question because I wasn't asking you to go through all the personnel, but you've answered the question. Why do you keep looking over at Mr. Karadzic when I ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I can't say I even noticed Mr. Karadzic sitting there. It may have been a perfectly automatic reaction. But if you mind, perhaps I should turn around and sit in such a way that I'm facing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can look however you want. I was just wondering why you were looking over there when I ask you questions. So just to make it short, basically the command chain of civilian -- of your staff in Bratunac went through Zvornik and then up to the republican staff in Pale, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: As for civilian protection, is my understanding correct, yes. The municipal civilian protection staff in Bratunac also had a regional staff in Zvornik and another one at the republican level. So that was the chain of command and the links.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: The way it operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Drinska Street number 13 in Bratunac. That's the street where the Vihor bus company is located on, right? Drinska Street.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Drinska Street number 13. That's interesting. Drinska Street number 13 is my family home. The last couple of months perhaps or last year the street numbers were changed around. So our home is now number 21, and Vihor, I can't really say, but it could be street number 13 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. My question wasn't clear. Drinska Street number 13 is where you used to live, correct, in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My mother is still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And you lived there during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I would spend the occasional night there during the war, but normally I live in Ljubovija, which is in Serbia. I bought some land there in February 1987 and subsequently built a home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I just ask you that, because in your sworn statements to the Republika Srpska MUP, and we'll look at them later maybe, you listed your address where you lived at Drinska Street Bratunac, not Serbia like we see in your statement here today.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this. We have five houses in Bratunac, the Tesics, and I myself own a house at this address. That's a big home where my youngest brother lives, and there is a smaller house, middle-sized house where my mother lives, and the first house where --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: -- we were born.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Where were you living in July 1995? You listed in your MUP statements of 2003 Bratunac. Were you living in Bratunac in July 1995 during that very difficult period for Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: For the most part, more often than not, I slept in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: At the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
