utterances.text: Right. And when you weren't in your office, the last time I'm going to ask it, were you sleeping in Bratunac in, say, July 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Those were critical days, and for sure I was at my office. Almost certainly I spent every night there, although from time to time I also went home to Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P04308 on the screen, please. That is an aerial of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, the witness who testified just before you, Branimir Tesic, is he related to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: We are brothers, both paternal and maternal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It could also be "cousins" in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already spoken about this. When he said that he had five houses, he mentioned that, but it didn't make it into the transcript. When he mentioned that the house where his mother lives, "that belonged to his brother who testified before me." That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page 282, please, in e-court. All right. Take a moment to look at this, sir. It's an aerial view of Bratunac, and you can see the road on the bottom right leads to Potocari. The one on the top heads off towards Ljubovija, Serbia. And then we can see marked the Hotel Fontana with a red line, the police station with a red line where your brother worked, the Vuk Karadzic school and the stadium. So could you, and the usher will help you, could you point to and put an M on the municipality building where your office was, because that's not marked clearly. If you can find it. Their Honours have been there. I just want to make this clear.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: What do you want me to mark? What do you want me to show? I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The municipality building where your office was. It's right up the street from the Vuk Karadzic school; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I can't really see too well. What is this? Well, it was right in the centre. I don't know what exactly you want me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, if you're having problem with the aerial, it was right down the street from the Vuk Karadzic school towards the centre where the mayor's office and the a -- is.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you help, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we zoom in a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, maybe if we could zoom in and maybe since there are some markings there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. We can lose it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Once again. Can you zoom bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you see the Vuk Karadzic school is marked with that red line.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. This is the school, and then down here that leads towards Vihor. Well, it's right here somewhere. I don't know exactly which building. It's a low building, rather long. Before the war the address was Marsala Tita Street 48. I don't know what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just leave that. That's fine. And Ljupko Ilic's office was also in that municipality building, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I want talk about some of those critical days, as you called them. This is from paragraph 41 of your statement. You said: "On the night of 13 or 14 July, 1995, I saw several buses loaded with Muslims in the town of Bratunac. At the time, I thought these people were from Potocari and could not be transported at night so they stopped there until daybreak. I did not hear that soldiers had abused anyone because there were no soldiers in the city, only the elderly women and children. I did not hear either that people were killed on buses, playgrounds, or streets. Over the next days I learned from Ljupko Ilic that there were several Muslim corpses in the Vuk Karadzic primary school." So we'll talk about 13 July in a minute, but something that's not in your statement at all is that the previous day, 12 July, you went to Potocari, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You went there around noon.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Let me try to recall that. After the meeting -- well, it wasn't quite a meeting, but General Mladic asked me to come to the command. He issued certain orders. And after that, perhaps sometime around noon, I can't recall exactly, I went to Potocari to see and check whether the situation was really as General Mladic said it was. He said that there was some 20.000 people, women, and children. Should I go on? I went to Potocari with the president of the Executive Council, Srbislav Davidovic, nicknamed Buco. We went in my private car. I went there and I really saw for myself that there were as many people as he said. I had some experience with assessing numbers, because I frequently went to football matches when I was a student, the Red Star club matches, and I could judge because the stadium would fill with a number of people and you could judge. So there were about -- at least 20.000 people, maybe even more there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: In Potocari I stayed for perhaps 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And did you notice that there were as reported in the MUP reports of that day virtually no men of military age present in the crowd?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, that depends. Well, they looked miserable. Maybe they were young. Well, not young. In those wartime years, even men of 60 years of age were conscripts, but there were people who were aged 30 or 40 or 50, and there were also a lot of women and children, but I don't know if they were military aged or able-bodied men or not, whether they were conscripts or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But it was overwhelmingly women and children and the elderly, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I think -- I think so. Most people were elderly. People 40, 50 years of age. As for able bodied young men who could carry their rifle every day, I don't think they were there. There were a few of them. Because they took another route. They did a breakthrough towards Tuzla some 15-16.000 of them. Those who wanted to fight --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't mean to cut you off but I don't have much time and you answered my question, thank you. You described that scene in your testimony at 7814, line 18, as a scene of suffering and as a humanitarian catastrophe. And that's true when you testified about that, isn't it? That's the way it looked to you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know what your intentions were. I've got about a half hour left, I think of my hour. I've got another topic. I'd rather just start that new topic tomorrow or we could go for four minutes if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's adjourn. Let's adjourn for today. Mr. Tesic, we'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
